standard: Every source the plant records cite, joined once so the plants section of the Evidence panel quotes a source exactly the way the building card and the wildlife list do.

andreas_1884_v1.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.

bowles_mcbride_1994_barrens.citation: Bowles, Marlin L. and Jeanette L. McBride. Presettlement Barrens in the Glaciated Prairie Region of Illinois. Proceedings of the North American Conference on Savannas and Barrens (Midwest Oak Savanna Conferences), 1994.
what_it_does_not_supply: tree densities per hectare - this paper gives none, so the savanna and woodland density figures in the zone records come from the seven-county Public Land Survey analysis instead

chicagology_prefire273.citation: "Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology. Transcribing the Chicago Magazine of 15 May 1857 — the account of the Wolf's Point settlement built on George Davis's 1832 drawing and on Gurdon S. Hubbard's own description of the place as he found it in 1818 — with A. T. Andreas and modern editorial matter around it.

transcribes.work: Chicago Magazine, 'Wolf's Point' — the account of the settlement at the forks, engraved from George Davis's 1832 drawing and incorporating Gurdon S. Hubbard's description of Chicago as he first saw it in 1818
transcribes.note: Carries the Miller House's log construction ('a log structure partly sided') and the Wolf Point Tavern's ('partly log and partly frame'), the fact of a frame element on each, and — through Hubbard — the marshy river-shore strip that grades the south division's marsh surface in terrain_spec.json. Twenty-five years after the fact, from a resident's drawing and a named witness speaking to the writer: rung 2.

chicagology_prefire274.citation: "Fort Dearborn I." Chicagology, transcribing Chicago Magazine, March 1857, with a Whistler plan of 1808, a Kinzie-supplied view of the first fort, and a 1902 Lawrence C. Earle mural.

transcribes.work: Chicago Magazine, 'Fort Dearborn I' — the account of the first fort and of the site it stood on, printed under its own attribution line and illustrated with a view 'through the kindness of Mrs. J. H. Kinzie, who furnished the sketch'
transcribes.note: Carries the landform this project's e1830_natural and e1834_harbor_cut epochs cite: the flattened mound half-surrounded by the river, standing 'as high as any other point'; the white sand hills north and south; and the long low sandy barrier ridge that deflected the river south 'for nearly half a mile' before the cut. Recollection of ground within the writer's own and his informants' memory, twenty-odd years after: the same rung as the May installment, on the same serial's method. Its 1803-1812 narrative is compilation, is not recollection, and is cited by nothing here.

what_it_supplies: the fort platform as a landform — a flattened mound, curved river on three sides, as high as any other point in the quadrant
the sandy barrier ridge between the deflected river and the lake, running south nearly half a mile
the white sand hills north and south of the river mouth
that the old southward channel's mouth was choked by sand bars, obstructing the smallest sail vessels
what_it_does_not_supply: the fort of 1835 — this installment stops at the 1812 massacre and the fort it describes is the FIRST fort, demolished that year
any dimension, plan or outline of either fort; the Whistler 1808 plan is reproduced as a picture and is not read here
a usable date for the harbour cut: it says 1838, against Andreas's works of 1833-34, and Andreas is followed
any elevation in feet — 'as high as any other point' is a comparison, not a measurement, and the modelled box's total relief is 4.30 ft

chicagology_prefire278.citation: "Town of Chicago." Chicagology. Transcribing the Inter Ocean of 22 July 1883 — 'Old Chicago: The Town in 1833', which carries both the town's incorporation record and 'The Old Western Hotel', an interview feature with named old settlers who used the house.

transcribes.work: Inter Ocean, 'Old Chicago: The Town in 1833' — the section headed 'The Old Western Hotel: First Frame House on the West Side', with the reporter's description of the surviving fragment and interviews with old settlers and with the builder's son
transcribes.note: Carries all four Western Hotel claims in this dataset — the farmers' and teamsters' house, W. H. Stow as builder and proprietor, the original two storeys, and the large stable and wagon yard with entrances from both streets — and it carries the dispute over the build date that keeps the dated range at `inferred`. Men recalling a house they used: rung 2.

cowles_1901.citation: Cowles, Henry Chandler. The Physiographic Ecology of Chicago and Vicinity; A Study of the Origin, Development, and Classification of Plant Societies. Botanical Gazette 31 (1901): 73-108, 145-182.

dollard_2018_beach_pea.citation: Dollard, John J., Jr. Experimental reintroduction of state-endangered beach pea (Lathyrus japonicus) to Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore. Park Science 34, no. 1 (2018): 47-53. National Park Service.
what_it_does_not_supply: historical vegetation; it is a 2010s restoration study, and nothing in it attests the 1835 Chicago lakefront

drloih_chicago_name.citation: The Origin and Meaning of the Name Chicago. Dr. Loih Journal, December 2016.

fpdcc_ecosystems.citation: Forest Preserves of Cook County. A Tour of Our Ecosystems.

idnr_tallgrass_plantlist.citation: Illinois Department of Natural Resources. Tall Prairie: Requirements and Plant Lists.
what_it_does_not_supply: bloom time or height - the page has no such column, so nothing about July phenology may be cited to it

kinzie_waubun_1856.citation: Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.

mcbride_bowles_2007.citation: McBride, Jeanette L. and Marlin L. Bowles. Searching the Public Land Survey for Illinois Natural History. The Morton Arboretum, December 2007.
what_it_supplies: regional species proportions and tree densities per hectare
the structural argument that even ground called timber was mostly open
what_it_does_not_supply: any vegetation record for the 640 m box at the forks itself - the nearest quoted survey line is about 2.5 km north
herbaceous species lists; the Public Land Survey recorded trees and land types, not forbs

mnfi_open_dunes.citation: Michigan Natural Features Inventory. Open Dunes (natural community abstract). Michigan State University Extension.

swenson_1991.citation: Swenson, John F. Chicagoua/Chicago: The Origin, Meaning, and Etymology of a Place Name. Illinois Historical Journal 84, no. 4 (Winter 1991): 235-248.

swink_wilhelm_1994.citation: Swink, Floyd and Gerould Wilhelm. Plants of the Chicago Region, 4th edition. Indiana Academy of Science, Indianapolis, 1994. Extended by Wilhelm, Gerould and Laura Rericha, Flora of the Chicago Region: A Floristic and Ecological Synthesis, Indiana Academy of Science, 2017.
what_it_supplies: which species belong to which Chicago-region community
what_it_does_not_supply: any record of what grew on the Chicago town site in 1835; a species on its regional list is inferred for this site, never documented, unless a period account names it

white_1978_inai.citation: White, John. Illinois Natural Areas Inventory Technical Report, Volume 1: Survey Methods and Results. Illinois Natural Areas Inventory, Urbana, 1978.
what_it_does_not_supply: any statement about Chicago in 1835; it classifies surviving natural areas surveyed in the 1970s, which is why species drawn from it are inferred for the site unless a period account names them

white_1994_savanna_terms.citation: White, John. How the Terms Savanna, Barrens, and Oak Openings Were Used in Early Illinois. Proceedings of the North American Conference on Savannas and Barrens (Midwest Oak Savanna Conferences), 1994.

wright_1834.citation: Wright, J. S. Chicago, drawn by J. S. Wright according to survey. New York: P. A. Mesier's Lith., 1834.
